Testing Real Crypto, Not Mocks

Every unit test suite so far mocked something out. These two are the first that deliberately don't.

Every unit test suite this project has written until now mocked something away from the thing under test — Prisma, most often (Lesson 2's jest.unstable_mockModule topic), so a test could focus on one function's own logic without a real database involved. password.test.js and jwt.test.js break that pattern on purpose:

// Figure 4.15: real bcrypt, no mock in sight (tests/unit/password.test.js, excerpt)
import { hashPassword, verifyPassword } from '../../src/utils/password.js';

it('verifyPassword accepts the correct password against its own hash', async () => {
  const hash = await hashPassword('password123');

  expect(await verifyPassword('password123', hash)).toBe(true);
});

There's nothing to mock here in the first place — hashPassword and verifyPassword don't touch Prisma, the network, or anything else this project would want isolated. The whole point of this test is "does real bcrypt hashing and comparing actually work the way this project depends on it working" — faking bcrypt out would leave nothing real under test at all. The same reasoning applies to jwt.test.js: it signs and verifies a real token against the real JWT_SECRET loaded from .env, checking that signToken/verifyToken (Lesson 4's JWT topic) genuinely round-trip a payload, and genuinely reject a tampered one.

Both suites still run fast — bcrypt's SALT_ROUNDS (this lesson's hashing topic) was chosen for real login latency, not test-suite latency, but even at that cost a handful of hashes in a test file is milliseconds, not something worth engineering around.
